question: How should we plan for account and HCP data volumes during a life sciences CRM migration?
answer: Account and HCP volumes vary significantly by therapeutic area and commercial model. A specialty pharma organization may have 10K-50K target HCPs, while a primary care launch can reach 200K-500K accounts. These volumes directly impact territory calculation time (each territory realignment must recompute sharing rules across the entire hierarchy), sync payload size for mobile users (larger account universes mean longer initial sync and more data on-device), and API consumption during bulk data loads. Plan for peak volumes at launch plus 18-24 months of growth. During migration from Veeva CRM, map the Veeva account universe precisely — Veeva's TSF (Territory Staging File) often contains historical accounts that inflate counts beyond active targets. Filter to active-status accounts before sizing the target platform. Index any fields used in territory filter criteria or mobile sync scope queries to maintain sub-second query performance at scale.

question: How do visit and call record volumes grow over time, and what retention strategies apply?
answer: Visit/call record volumes grow predictably based on rep count and call frequency. A typical field rep generates 500-2000 visit records per year (6-10 calls per day, 200+ working days). For a 1,000-rep organization, that is 500K-2M new records annually. After 3-5 years, visit history can reach 5-10M records, causing query performance degradation on reports, dashboards, and mobile sync. Implement a tiered retention strategy: keep 12-18 months of detailed visit data in the primary object for active querying and mobile access, archive older records to a secondary custom object or external storage (Big Objects work well for this pattern on the target platform), and maintain summary/aggregate records for historical reporting. During migration from Veeva CRM, decide early whether to migrate full call history or only the active window — migrating 5+ years of Veeva call data is a common source of timeline overruns with minimal business value. The platform's async SOQL feature can query archived Big Object data without impacting transactional governor limits.

question: What are the content volume considerations for CLM presentations and approved content?
answer: CLM (Closed Loop Marketing) content volumes are the single largest driver of mobile storage and sync time. Individual CLM presentations range from 50MB for simple slide-based content to 2-8GB for interactive HTML5 presentations with embedded video. A typical brand team may have 10-30 active presentations, and a multi-brand organization can have 100+ active content items totaling 20-50GB. This directly impacts: (1) Initial device provisioning — first-time content download can take 30-60 minutes on WiFi, hours on cellular; (2) Ongoing sync — content updates trigger full presentation re-download, not delta sync; (3) Device storage — iPad models with 64GB storage can run critically low with large content libraries. Implement content lifecycle management: set expiration dates on all content, run quarterly purge cycles to remove expired/unused presentations, segment content by product team with different sync scopes so reps only download content for their assigned brands. When migrating from Veeva CRM, audit the Veeva Vault content library for active vs. archived presentations — organizations commonly have 3-5x more content in Vault than reps actually use.

question: How should we handle sample transaction volumes, especially during product launches?
answer: Sample transaction volumes spike dramatically during product launches — a new drug launch can generate 5-10x the normal sample transaction rate as reps distribute starter samples to build prescriber awareness. Normal steady-state is 3-8 sample transactions per rep per day; during launch periods this can reach 20-40 per day. This impacts: (1) Batch calculation jobs — sample limit recalculation must process all open-period transactions to determine remaining allocations, and at high volumes these jobs can exceed the 60-second synchronous timeout, requiring async batch processing; (2) Reconciliation — quarterly sample reconciliation compares physical inventory against transaction records across the entire rep population, and for organizations with 1,000+ reps this involves millions of records; (3) Compliance reporting — DEA/FDA audit trail requirements mean sample records cannot be purged, only archived. Plan the sample management data model with partitioning by sample lot and reconciliation period. After each reconciliation cycle completes and is signed off, archive closed-period transactions to reduce the active record set. During migration from Veeva CRM, carefully map Veeva's sample transaction states (Submitted, In Transit, Received, Discrepancy) to the target platform's equivalents — state mismatches cause compliance gaps.

question: What governor limits apply to life sciences CRM batch jobs like sample limits, activity plans, and territory alignment?
answer: The target platform enforces strict governor limits that directly affect life sciences batch operations. Key limits: (1) Batch Apex — each batch execution can process up to 2,000 records per chunk (default scope), with a maximum of 250,000 batch executions per 24 hours and 5 concurrent batch jobs per org. Sample limit calculation, activity plan attainment rollup, and territory realignment all compete for these slots. (2) Queueable chaining — queueable jobs can chain to one additional job in production (up to 5 in unit tests), limiting how you decompose long-running calculations. (3) Async apex — total async method invocations cannot exceed 250,000 per 24 hours per org (or number of licenses x 200, whichever is greater). For large organizations running nightly sample limit recalculation + weekly activity plan attainment + monthly territory realignment, this budget gets tight. Stagger batch jobs with at least 30-minute gaps between major operations. Use the BatchApexWorker pattern with configurable scope size — start at 200 records per chunk and tune based on the complexity of the per-record logic. Monitor with the AsyncApexJob object to detect jobs stuck in Queued or Preparing states.

question: How should SOQL queries be optimized for large life sciences CRM objects?
answer: SOQL query optimization is critical for objects that grow beyond 100K records — accounts, visits, sample transactions, and activity plan line items are the most common large objects in life sciences CRM. Key optimization strategies: (1) Selectivity — the query optimizer requires filters to be selective (matching less than 10% of total records for standard indexes, less than 5% for custom indexes, or less than 333,333 records for either). For visit objects with millions of records, ensure date range filters and status filters are indexed. (2) Custom indexes — request custom indexes on fields frequently used in WHERE clauses: Visit_Date__c, Account__c (lookup), Status__c, and Owner (standard). Composite indexes combining two fields can dramatically improve queries like 'SELECT Id FROM Visit WHERE Account__c = :acctId AND Visit_Date__c > :cutoff'. (3) Skinny tables — for very large objects (10M+ records), request skinny table creation from platform support to maintain a denormalized copy of frequently queried columns. (4) Mobile composite queries — mobile sync uses SOQL to determine the delta record set; non-selective sync queries cause full table scans and timeouts. Ensure the sync scope configuration includes selective filter criteria. When migrating from Veeva, note that Veeva's underlying SOQL performance characteristics are identical — existing Veeva query patterns that perform well will generally transfer, but custom report queries may need re-tuning after data volume changes.

question: What API limits apply to life sciences CRM implementations and how do they affect migrations?
answer: API call limits are allocated per 24-hour rolling window based on org edition and license count. Enterprise Edition orgs receive 1,000 calls per user license (minimum 15,000), with a hard cap. For a 1,000-user life sciences org, this typically means 100,000-1,000,000 daily API calls depending on edition and add-on purchases. Critical consumption points: (1) Data migration — Bulk API 2.0 processes up to 10,000 records per batch and is the recommended path for migration loads; it counts as a single API call per batch rather than per record. Migrating 5M records at 10K per batch requires only 500 API calls. (2) Integration endpoints — middleware syncing account master data, sample inventory, medical inquiry feeds, and territory files consume REST API calls. Each integration touchpoint should batch requests using composite API (up to 25 subrequests per call) or Bulk API for large payloads. (3) Mobile sync — each mobile sync cycle generates API calls for metadata checks and data retrieval; with 1,000 reps syncing 4-6 times daily, this alone can consume 20,000-30,000 daily calls. (4) Streaming API — use Platform Events for real-time updates (territory changes, sample allocation updates) instead of polling, which burns API calls. Monitor daily consumption via the API Usage page and set up alerts at 70% and 90% thresholds.

question: How should we manage storage limits for file-heavy life sciences CRM implementations?
answer: Storage is divided into data storage (records) and file storage (attachments, documents, content). Life sciences CRM implementations are disproportionately file-heavy due to CLM content, signature capture images, sample receipt attachments, and medical inquiry documents. Typical allocation: data storage starts at 10GB + 20MB per user; file storage starts at 10GB + 2GB per user. For a 1,000-user org: ~20GB data storage and ~2TB file storage baseline. Pain points: (1) CLM content stored as ContentVersion records consumes file storage rapidly — a single 500MB presentation uses 0.5GB, and a 100-presentation library consumes 50GB before versioning. Each content update creates a new ContentVersion, so storage grows with each publish cycle. (2) Signature captures from e-signatures on sample receipts and call reports generate 50-200KB image files per visit — 1M visits/year creates 50-200GB of signature files. (3) Content delivery network — for CLM content, consider external CDN hosting with platform references rather than storing full content natively. Set up storage monitoring dashboards and configure weekly email alerts. Implement automated archival: move signature images older than 2 years to external storage with platform references, purge expired CLM content versions (keep only current + one prior version), and compress medical inquiry attachments after case closure.

question: What determines initial sync time for mobile life sciences CRM apps, and how can it be reduced?
answer: Initial sync time is the single most common source of end-user complaints during life sciences CRM rollouts. Factors: (1) Data volume — sync downloads all records matching the user's territory/scope: accounts, contacts, addresses, visit history, sample inventory, CLM content, activity plans, and reference data. For a primary care rep with 500+ target accounts, this can be 50,000-100,000 records plus associated content. (2) Content download — CLM presentations are the bottleneck; 5-10GB of content requires 15-30 minutes on a strong WiFi connection. (3) Metadata — custom object definitions, page layouts, picklist values, and record types must be fetched before data sync begins. Complex orgs with 100+ custom objects add 2-5 minutes to metadata sync alone. Reduction strategies: (a) Pre-stage content on managed devices using MDM before distributing to reps. (b) Limit sync scope — use territory-based filters so reps only sync accounts in their territory, not the full org. (c) Phase the rollout — deploy metadata and reference data first, then content, then transactional data. (d) Use WiFi-only sync policy for initial setup to avoid cellular timeouts. (e) Set sync window expectations: communicate that initial setup requires 30-90 minutes on WiFi, and schedule it during a training session or overnight. Typical initial sync times: small org (100 accounts, minimal content) = 15-20 minutes; medium org (500 accounts, moderate content) = 45-60 minutes; large org (2000+ accounts, heavy content) = 90-120+ minutes.

question: What is the expected performance for ongoing delta sync, and when should a full re-sync be triggered?
answer: Ongoing delta (incremental) sync should complete in under 60 seconds for normal daily operations — this is the target for a rep syncing between calls throughout the day. Delta sync fetches only records modified since the last sync timestamp, which under normal conditions is a small set: new visits logged by the rep, account updates from data stewardship, sample inventory changes, and any territory or content updates. Factors that degrade delta sync: (1) Bulk data loads — a nightly account master refresh that touches 10,000+ accounts forces the next delta sync to process all of them, potentially taking 5-10 minutes. Schedule bulk loads during off-hours and communicate to field teams. (2) Territory realignment — a mid-cycle territory change reassigns accounts across reps, triggering large delta sets for affected users. (3) Content updates — publishing a new CLM presentation version triggers content re-download for all reps with that content assigned. Full re-sync (clearing local data and re-downloading everything) should be rare — only triggered by: app version upgrades that change the local schema, data corruption detected by checksum validation, or after extended offline periods (30+ days) where the delta window becomes too large. Full re-sync takes the same time as initial sync. Design the sync framework with a 'sync health' indicator that monitors delta sync duration trends and alerts when average sync time exceeds 2 minutes, signaling potential data volume or configuration issues.

question: How should offline database performance and memory be managed on mobile devices for life sciences CRM?
answer: Offline performance depends entirely on the local SQLite database efficiency and device memory management. Key considerations: (1) SQLite optimization — create indexes on all columns used in local queries: account name (for search), visit date (for calendar views), territory ID (for filtering), and status fields. Without indexes, account search across 10,000+ records takes 500ms+; with proper indexes, it drops to under 50ms. Use WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode for concurrent read/write performance. (2) Memory management on iPad — life sciences CRM apps typically consume 200-500MB of RAM during active use. iPad devices (especially 64GB models with 3-4GB RAM) can experience memory pressure when: the app holds large datasets in memory (e.g., loading all visit records for a calendar view instead of paginating), CLM presentation rendering allocates WebView memory for HTML5 content, and background sync operations run concurrently with UI operations. Implement aggressive memory release: free CLM WebView memory when presentations are dismissed, paginate all list views to 50 records per fetch, and use database cursors rather than loading full result sets. (3) Database size — the local SQLite database should stay under 500MB for responsive query performance; databases exceeding 1GB show measurable degradation in complex JOIN queries. Monitor on-device database size and trigger optimization (VACUUM, re-index) when it exceeds thresholds. Common memory leak sources: unreleased observation/notification listeners, retained closure references to large data objects, and WebView instances not properly deallocated after CLM playback.

question: What are the performance considerations for CLM content rendering on mobile devices?
answer: CLM presentation rendering performance directly affects the rep's in-office experience with HCPs — a slow-loading presentation during a physician visit is a critical usability failure. Performance targets: presentations should load to interactive state within 3 seconds, slide transitions should complete in under 300ms, and embedded videos should begin playback within 2 seconds. Factors affecting rendering: (1) HTML5 player performance — modern CLM content uses HTML5/JavaScript rather than PDF, enabling interactivity but requiring WebView rendering. Complex presentations with heavy CSS animations, embedded iframes, or large JavaScript bundles can overwhelm the WebView on older iPad models. Target WebView memory under 200MB per presentation. (2) Animation frame rates — interactive CLM content with animations should maintain 30fps minimum (60fps target). Test on the oldest supported device model, not the newest. (3) Video playback — embedded product videos should be transcoded to H.264 at 720p for mobile (not 1080p or 4K from the creative agency). A single 1080p video file can be 500MB+; 720p reduces to 100-200MB with minimal visible quality loss on iPad screen sizes. (4) Image optimization — CLM agencies frequently deliver presentations with unoptimized images (10MB+ per slide). Require image optimization as part of the content publishing pipeline: max 2MB per image, WebP format where supported, and lazy-loading for images below the fold. Implement a CLM performance testing protocol: load each presentation on the minimum-spec supported device over cellular connection and measure time-to-interactive.

question: How does territory hierarchy depth affect performance, and what is the optimal configuration?
answer: Territory hierarchy depth has a non-linear impact on sharing calculation performance. The target platform recalculates sharing rules whenever territory assignments change — each additional hierarchy level multiplies the number of sharing records that must be evaluated. Optimal configuration is 3-5 levels (e.g., Nation > Region > District > Territory). At 3 levels with 1,000 territories, sharing calculations complete in minutes. At 7+ levels, the same operation can take hours because each account's sharing must be evaluated against every ancestor territory in the hierarchy. Specific impacts: (1) Territory realignment — the quarterly realignment job that reassigns accounts across territories triggers a full sharing recalculation. For hierarchies deeper than 5 levels, this can exceed the 24-hour async processing window. (2) Role hierarchy interaction — territory hierarchy interacts with the role hierarchy for record access. Deep territory hierarchies combined with deep role hierarchies create a combinatorial explosion of sharing records. (3) Implicit sharing — each territory-account assignment creates implicit sharing records for all users in parent territories. With a 7-level hierarchy and 500K account-territory assignments, the sharing table can grow to tens of millions of rows. When migrating from Veeva CRM, note that Veeva typically uses a simpler territory model. Map Veeva's territory hierarchy to the target platform's territory management feature, and flatten any levels that exist only for Veeva reporting purposes but don't control data access.

question: How does page layout complexity affect form load time, and what are the recommended limits?
answer: Page layout complexity directly affects both web and mobile form rendering performance. Each visible field on a layout requires a metadata describe call, a data fetch, and a UI render cycle. Recommended limits: keep page layouts under 50 visible fields per layout (including all sections), limit related lists to 5 per layout with no more than 10 columns each, and restrict lookup fields to 10 per layout (each lookup triggers an additional SOQL query for the reference display name). Measured impact: a layout with 30 fields loads in 1-2 seconds; 50 fields takes 2-4 seconds; 80+ fields can take 6-10 seconds and causes measurable user abandonment. For mobile: the penalty is amplified because the mobile app must also download layout metadata during sync and render fields in a smaller viewport. Mobile-specific page layouts should be even leaner — 25-35 fields maximum, with progressive disclosure (expandable sections) for less-used fields. Life sciences-specific considerations: (1) Visit/call report layouts tend to accumulate fields over time as commercial operations adds tracking requirements — audit quarterly and archive unused fields. (2) Account layouts with multiple address types, affiliations, and license information can easily exceed 80 fields — use tabbed or accordion layouts to defer rendering. (3) Custom Lightning components embedded in layouts add to load time; each component initializes independently. When migrating from Veeva, use the migration as an opportunity to rationalize layouts — Veeva implementations commonly have 100+ field layouts that were never optimized.

question: How should batch jobs be scheduled to avoid conflicts and optimize processing windows?
answer: Life sciences CRM implementations typically run 5-10 recurring batch jobs that compete for the platform's 5 concurrent batch job slots and 250,000 daily async execution limit. Critical batch jobs and recommended scheduling: (1) Sample limit recalculation — runs nightly to update remaining sample allocations based on day's transactions. Schedule at 11 PM-1 AM local time (after reps finish logging). Duration: 15-45 minutes for 1,000 reps. (2) Activity plan attainment calculation — rolls up completed activities against plan targets. Schedule at 1-3 AM. Duration: 30-90 minutes depending on plan complexity and rep count. (3) Territory realignment — runs quarterly or on-demand when territory files are loaded. Schedule during weekends. Duration: 2-8 hours for large orgs. Must not overlap with any other batch job. (4) Data quality/deduplication jobs — weekly account matching and merge candidate identification. Schedule Saturday 2-6 AM. (5) Compliance reporting — weekly or monthly aggregation of sample transactions, adverse event reports, and call activity for regulatory submissions. Schedule Sunday 4-8 AM. Scheduling principles: (a) Never run two large batch jobs concurrently — use the Schedulable interface with CronTrigger checks that verify no other critical job is running before starting. (b) Build in 30-minute buffers between jobs for overrun. (c) Implement a job monitoring framework that sends alerts when any batch job exceeds its expected duration by 50%. (d) Use the Flex Queue for overflow — jobs submitted when all 5 slots are full enter the flex queue (up to 100 jobs) and execute as slots free up.

question: What is the recommended performance testing strategy for a life sciences CRM implementation?
answer: Performance testing for life sciences CRM must go beyond standard load testing because the unique combination of mobile offline, batch processing, and regulatory compliance creates failure modes that only appear at production scale. Testing strategy: (1) Data volume testing — load the test environment with production-representative data volumes (accounts, visits, samples, content). Never test with a 1,000-record sandbox when production will have 5M records. Use the Bulk API to seed test data, targeting 80-100% of expected Year 1 production volume. (2) Concurrent user simulation — simulate realistic usage patterns: 60% of reps syncing between 7-9 AM (morning sync storm), field reps logging visits throughout the day (steady-state), and managers running reports at month-end (query-heavy). For a 1,000-rep org, test with 200-300 concurrent API sessions. (3) Offline-to-online transition testing — the most under-tested scenario. Simulate a rep working offline for 4-8 hours (creating 10-15 visits, capturing signatures, logging samples) then reconnecting. The sync-up must handle conflict resolution, attachment upload, and data validation without data loss. Test with concurrent offline users syncing simultaneously. (4) Batch job stress testing — run the sample limit calculation and activity plan attainment jobs against production-volume data and measure duration, governor limit consumption, and error rates. (5) Integration endpoint testing — test middleware throughput with realistic payload sizes (account master files, territory files, sample inventory feeds). Use dedicated performance testing environments with production-equivalent compute allocation — sandbox orgs often have reduced compute that produces misleading results.

question: What key metrics should be monitored for ongoing life sciences CRM performance health?
answer: Establish a performance monitoring dashboard covering these metrics with defined thresholds and alerting: (1) Mobile sync time — track P50, P90, and P99 delta sync duration. Target: P50 under 30s, P90 under 60s, P99 under 120s. Alert when P90 exceeds 90s for 3 consecutive days — this indicates growing data volume or sync scope misconfiguration. (2) API response time — monitor REST API response times for the top 10 most-called endpoints. Target: P95 under 2 seconds. Track daily API consumption against the org limit and alert at 70% threshold. (3) Batch job duration — track execution time for each recurring batch job. Alert when any job exceeds 150% of its trailing 30-day average duration. Track batch failures separately — a sample limit batch that fails silently leaves reps with stale allocation data, which is a compliance risk. (4) Mobile app memory usage — instrument the mobile app to report peak memory consumption per session. Target: under 500MB peak. Alert when the 7-day rolling average exceeds 400MB — memory creep indicates a leak that will eventually cause crashes. (5) Crash-free session rate — target 99.9%+ crash-free sessions. Any drop below 99.5% warrants immediate investigation. Segment by device model and OS version to identify platform-specific issues. (6) Page load time — track Lightning page load times for the top 5 most-visited pages (account detail, visit log, call report, dashboard home, sample management). Target: under 3 seconds for initial load. (7) SOQL query performance — use the query plan tool to review the top 20 slowest queries weekly. Any non-selective query on an object with 100K+ records is a ticking time bomb.

question: What are the most common performance anti-patterns in life sciences CRM implementations?
answer: These anti-patterns appear repeatedly in life sciences CRM implementations and cause production performance issues that are expensive to remediate: (1) Too many triggers on the Visit object — the visit/call report is the most-written object in life sciences CRM, and it commonly accumulates 5-10 triggers over time (sample validation, coaching score calculation, activity plan attainment update, compliance checks, integration callouts). Each trigger fires on every insert/update, and trigger order is non-deterministic. Consolidate to a single trigger with a handler framework that controls execution order and allows disabling individual handlers. (2) SOQL in loops — the most common governor limit violation. Example: iterating over visit records and querying account details inside the loop instead of pre-fetching with a single collection query. This pattern hits the 100 SOQL query limit and fails at scale even if it works during testing with small data. (3) Non-selective queries on large objects — querying the visit object with WHERE Status = 'Planned' when 40% of records are Planned (non-selective) forces a full table scan. Add compound filters (Status + Date range) or request custom indexes. (4) Unindexed fields in WHERE clauses — custom fields used in report filters, list view filters, or sync scope queries are not indexed by default. Every custom field used in a WHERE clause on an object with 100K+ records needs an explicit index request. (5) Synchronous callouts in triggers — making HTTP callouts to external systems (sample inventory, medical information) synchronously in a trigger blocks the transaction and fails under load. Use Platform Events or Queueable Apex for async processing. (6) Unbounded related list queries — loading all visit history for an account without a date range filter. For key accounts with 5+ years of visit history (1,000+ records), this causes page timeout. Always apply date range limits to historical queries. (7) Over-fetching in mobile sync — syncing all fields on all objects when the mobile UI only displays a subset. Configure mobile sync to fetch only the fields needed for offline display and editing.
